claim: Ibrutinib was first approved by the FDA in 2013.
source: Ibrutinib (IMBRUVICA), has revolutionized the treatment of the B-cell malignancy, CLL (Burger et al., 2015). Ibrutinib is a covalent active site inhibitor of the multi-domain B-cell kinase, BTK (Figure 1a), that was first approved by the FDA in 2013 (Davids and Brown, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davids and Brown, 2014.

claim: Inhibition of BTK disrupts signaling downstream of the B-cell receptor (BCR).
source: Inhibition of BTK disrupts signaling downstream of the B-cell receptor (BCR), a pathway on which the survival of CLL cells is dependent (Honigberg et al., 2010; Herman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Honigberg et al., 2010 and Herman et al., 2011.

claim: CLL cell survival is dependent on the B-cell receptor pathway.
source: Inhibition of BTK disrupts signaling downstream of the B-cell receptor (BCR), a pathway on which the survival of CLL cells is dependent (Honigberg et al., 2010; Herman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Honigberg et al., 2010 and Herman et al., 2011.

claim: Acalabrutinib (CALQUENCE) is a clinically approved BTK inhibitor.
source: The success of Ibrutinib has spurred the development of other BTKi including the now clinically approved BTK inhibitors: Acalabrutinib (CALQUENCE), Zanubrutinib (BRUKINSA), Tirabrutinib/ONO-4059 (VELEXBRU), Pirtobrutinib/LOXO-405 (JAYPIRCA) and Orelabrutinib (HIBRUKA) (Rozkiewicz et al., 2023; Shirley, 2022; Montoya and Thompson, 2023; Kueffer et al., 2021; Frustaci et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Rozkiewicz et al., 2023.

claim: All clinically approved BTK inhibitors except Pirtobrutinib are covalent active site inhibitors that bind to BTK C481 residue.
source: All of the clinically approved BTKi (with the exception of Pirtobrutinib) are covalent active site inhibitors that bind to BTK C481 residue within the kinase active site.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Pirtobrutinib is currently the first and only clinically approved non-covalent BTK active site inhibitor.
source: Pirtobrutinib is currently the first and only clinically approved non-covalent BTK active site inhibitor (Montoya and Thompson, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Montoya and Thompson, 2023.

claim: All clinically approved BTK inhibitors in this study completely block nucleotide binding.
source: Importantly, all clinically approved BTK inhibitors in this study, covalent and non-covalent, completely block nucleotide binding.
evidence: The claim is stated as an important finding in the manuscript.

claim: BTK inhibitors are being used to treat B-cell malignancies such as Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, and Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL).
source: While BTKi are highly effective in the treatment of CLL, they are also being used to treat other B-cell malignancies such as Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) and are being evaluated in the treatment of multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis (Rozkiewicz et al., 2023; Mendes-Bastos et al., 2022; Robak and Robak, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rozkiewicz et al., 2023; Mendes-Bastos et al., 2022; Robak and Robak, 2022.

claim: BTK inhibitors are being evaluated in the treatment of multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis.
source: While BTKi are highly effective in the treatment of CLL, they are also being used to treat other B-cell malignancies such as Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) and are being evaluated in the treatment of multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis (Rozkiewicz et al., 2023; Mendes-Bastos et al., 2022; Robak and Robak, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rozkiewicz et al., 2023; Mendes-Bastos et al., 2022; Robak and Robak, 2022.

claim: Recent clinical trial data indicate that BTK inhibitors differ in their effectiveness in treating various conditions.
source: Indeed, recent clinical trial data comparing one BTKi to another indicate that BTKi differ in their effectiveness in treating various conditions (Byrd et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2023; Lovell et al., 2022; Buske et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byrd et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2023; Lovell et al., 2022; Buske et al., 2023.

claim: Ibrutinib binding to the BTK kinase active site leads to a shift in the conformational ensemble of full-length BTK towards an open conformation.
source: Ibrutinib binding to the BTK kinase active site leads to a shift in the conformational ensemble of full-length BTK towards an open conformation where the regulatory SRC homology (SH3 and SH2) domains are released from the 'back' surface of the kinase domain, disrupting the closed autoinhibited conformation of the full-length protein (Figure 1b, Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Allosteric conformational changes upon drug binding have been shown to alter protein-ligand interactions in other systems with functional consequences in vivo.
source: Allosteric conformational changes upon drug binding have been shown to alter protein-ligand interactions in other systems with functional consequences in vivo (Sonti et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2017; Skora et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sonti et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2017; Skora et al., 2013.

claim: Resistance to BTK inhibitors typically develops in patients approximately 2 years after the start of treatment.
source: Despite the success of BTKi in CLL, a recurring problem is the development of BTKi resistance. Resistance typically develops in patients ~2 y after the start of BTK inhibitor treatment (Sedlarikova et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sedlarikova et al., 2020.

claim: Most CLL patients that stop responding to BTK inhibitors develop mutations within Btk or in the substrate of BTK: Phospholipase C gamma 2 (PLCγ2).
source: Analysis of CLL patients that stop responding to BTKi has revealed that most develop mutations within Btk or in the substrate of BTK: Phospholipase C gamma 2 (PLCγ2) (Maddocks et al., 2015; Ahn et al., 2017; Woyach et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maddocks et al., 2015; Ahn et al., 2017; Woyach et al., 2014.

claim: The specific resistance mutations that develop in Btk depend on the specific BTK inhibitor used.
source: Interestingly, the specific resistance mutations that develop in Btk seem to be dependent on the specific BTKi used (Woyach et al., 2014; Blombery et al., 2022; Furman et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2022; Jackson et al., 2023; Handunnetti et al., 2019; Woyach et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Woyach et al., 2014; Blombery et al., 2022; Furman et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2022; Jackson et al., 2023; Handunnetti et al., 2019; Woyach et al., 2019.

claim: Patients treated with the reversible inhibitor Pirtobrutinib do not develop mutations in C481.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, patients treated with the reversible inhibitor Pirtobrutinib do not develop mutations in C481 (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1d showing mutation prevalence data.

claim: Patients treated with Pirtobrutinib develop kinase active site mutations including BTK T474I and L528W.
source: Instead, they develop other kinase active site mutations including BTK T474I and L528W (Figure 1c and d; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022 and reference to Figure 1c and d.

claim: 90% or more of CLL patients treated with Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib develop mutations in BTK C481.
source: In contrast, 90% or more of CLL patients treated with Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib develop mutations in BTK C481 (Figure 1d, Supplementary file 1, Maddocks et al., 2015; Ahn et al., 2017; Woyach et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maddocks et al., 2015; Ahn et al., 2017; Woyach et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mutations of BTK C481 to residues other than serine (C481F/Y/R) occur at a much lower frequency than C481S.
source: While mutation of BTK C481 to residues other than serine have also been reported (C481F/Y/R), they occur at a much lower frequency (Nakhoda et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakhoda et al., 2023.

claim: BTK T474 and L528 are rarely (if ever) mutated in Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib-treated CLL patients.
source: Additionally, other sites within BTK such as T474 and L528 are rarely (if ever) mutated in Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib-treated CLL patients (Figure 1d, Supplementary file 1, Maddocks et al., 2015; Woyach et al., 2014; Blombery et al., 2022; Woyach et al., 2017; Kanagal-Shamanna et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maddocks et al., 2015; Woyach et al., 2014; Blombery et al., 2022; Woyach et al., 2017; Kanagal-Shamanna et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BTK T474 and L528 are frequently mutated in CLL patients treated with the covalent inhibitors Zanubrutinib and Tirabrutinib.
source: Surprisingly, BTK T474 and L528 are frequently mutated in CLL patients treated with the covalent inhibitors Zanubrutinib and Tirabrutinib (Figure 1d, Blombery et al., 2022; Jackson et al., 2023; Handunnetti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blombery et al., 2022; Jackson et al., 2023; Handunnetti et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: BTK T474I and L528W are found at almost equal or higher frequency compared to C481S in Zanubrutinib and Tirabrutinib treated patients.
source: BTK T474I and L528W are found at almost equal or higher frequency compared to C481S in these patients (Figure 1d, Supplementary file 1, Blombery et al., 2022; Jackson et al., 2023; Handunnetti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blombery et al., 2022; Jackson et al., 2023; Handunnetti et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In Zanubrutinib-treated patients, the L528W mutation was often present together with the C481S mutation (on different alleles), with L528W present at a higher allelic frequency compared to C481S.
source: Moreover, in Zanubrutinib-treated patients, the L528W mutation was often present together with the C481S mutation (on different alleles), and with the L528W mutation present at a higher allelic frequency compared to C481S (Handunnetti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Handunnetti et al., 2019.

claim: Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Tirabrutinib disrupted the autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK similarly to Ibrutinib but to varying degrees.
source: Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Tirabrutinib disrupted the autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK similarly to Ibrutinib but did so to varying degrees.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: Acalabrutinib and Tirabrutinib altered the dynamics of the kinase G-helix, a region previously characterized as the PLCγ substrate docking site.
source: Interestingly, Acalabrutinib and Tirabrutinib altered the dynamics of the kinase G-helix, a region that has been previously characterized as the PLCγ substrate docking site (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: Pirtobrutinib stabilized the compact autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
source: Pirtobrutinib on the other hand stabilized the compact autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK and is the first BTK inhibitor observed to do so.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: Pirtobrutinib is the first BTK inhibitor observed to stabilize the compact autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
source: Pirtobrutinib on the other hand stabilized the compact autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK and is the first BTK inhibitor observed to do so.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The catalytically inactive BTK L528W mutant activated the SRC kinase HCK.
source: Additionally, we probed the mechanism of action of the BTK resistance mutations T474I and L528W. We show that the catalytically inactive BTK L528W mutant activated the SRC kinase HCK and that this activation is dependent on the proline-rich region within BTK.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: Activation of HCK by the BTK L528W mutant is dependent on the proline-rich region within BTK.
source: We show that the catalytically inactive BTK L528W mutant activated the SRC kinase HCK and that this activation is dependent on the proline-rich region within BTK.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The BTK T474I mutation disrupted binding to Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib.
source: The BTK T474I mutation disrupted binding to Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib and likely evades the action of these drugs due to reduced binding to these inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The BTK T474I mutation likely evades the action of Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib due to reduced binding to these inhibitors.
source: The BTK T474I mutation disrupted binding to Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib and likely evades the action of these drugs due to reduced binding to these inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The development of the C481S resistance mutation is dependent on the half-life of the inhibitor.
source: Furthermore, we provide an explanation for the mutational bias observed in patients treated with different covalent BTKi. The development of the C481S resistance mutation is dependent on the half-life of the inhibitor which likely explains the low prevalence of the C481S resistance mutation in patients treated with the covalent inhibitors Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib (which have a long half-life) as compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib (which have a short half-life).
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The half-life of the inhibitor explains the low prevalence of the C481S resistance mutation in patients treated with Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib.
source: The development of the C481S resistance mutation is dependent on the half-life of the inhibitor which likely explains the low prevalence of the C481S resistance mutation in patients treated with the covalent inhibitors Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib (which have a long half-life) as compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib (which have a short half-life).
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib have a long half-life.
source: The development of the C481S resistance mutation is dependent on the half-life of the inhibitor which likely explains the low prevalence of the C481S resistance mutation in patients treated with the covalent inhibitors Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib (which have a long half-life) as compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib (which have a short half-life).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib have a short half-life.
source: The development of the C481S resistance mutation is dependent on the half-life of the inhibitor which likely explains the low prevalence of the C481S resistance mutation in patients treated with the covalent inhibitors Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib (which have a long half-life) as compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib (which have a short half-life).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: The catalytic kinase domain of BTK can adopt an active or inactive conformation in solution.
source: The catalytic kinase domain of BTK can adopt an active or inactive conformation in solution and previous studies have shown that inhibitor binding can stabilize one or more of these conformations (Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibitor binding can stabilize one or more conformations of the BTK kinase domain.
source: The catalytic kinase domain of BTK can adopt an active or inactive conformation in solution and previous studies have shown that inhibitor binding can stabilize one or more of these conformations (Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: The switch from an inactive to an active kinase conformation involves the inward movement of the C-helix from an inactive 'αC out' to the active 'αC in' position.
source: These changes include the inward movement of the C-helix from an inactive 'αC out' to the active 'αC in' position, changes in the side chain rotamer conformation of BTK W395, formation of a conserved BTK K430:E445 salt bridge and unfurling of the collapsed activation loop, leading to the exposure of the conserved Y551 on the activation loop for phosphorylation (Figure 2a, Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The switch from an inactive to an active kinase conformation involves changes in the side chain rotamer conformation of BTK W395.
source: These changes include the inward movement of the C-helix from an inactive 'αC out' to the active 'αC in' position, changes in the side chain rotamer conformation of BTK W395, formation of a conserved BTK K430:E445 salt bridge and unfurling of the collapsed activation loop, leading to the exposure of the conserved Y551 on the activation loop for phosphorylation (Figure 2a, Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The switch from an inactive to an active kinase conformation involves formation of a conserved BTK K430:E445 salt bridge.
source: These changes include the inward movement of the C-helix from an inactive 'αC out' to the active 'αC in' position, changes in the side chain rotamer conformation of BTK W395, formation of a conserved BTK K430:E445 salt bridge and unfurling of the collapsed activation loop, leading to the exposure of the conserved Y551 on the activation loop for phosphorylation (Figure 2a, Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The switch from an inactive to an active kinase conformation involves unfurling of the collapsed activation loop, leading to the exposure of the conserved Y551 on the activation loop for phosphorylation.
source: These changes include the inward movement of the C-helix from an inactive 'αC out' to the active 'αC in' position, changes in the side chain rotamer conformation of BTK W395, formation of a conserved BTK K430:E445 salt bridge and unfurling of the collapsed activation loop, leading to the exposure of the conserved Y551 on the activation loop for phosphorylation (Figure 2a, Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Crystal structures of the BTK kinase domain in complex with Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, or Pirtobrutinib show that each inhibitor stabilizes the kinase domain in an inactive conformation similar to that of Ibrutinib-bound BTK.
source: Crystal structures of the BTK kinase domain in complex with Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, or Pirtobrutinib are available and show that each of these BTK inhibitors stabilizes the kinase domain in an inactive conformation similar to that of Ibrutinib-bound BTK (Figure 2b–f, Joseph et al., 2020; Lin and Andreotti, 2023; Gomez et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Joseph et al., 2020; Lin and Andreotti, 2023; Gomez et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 2b-f.

claim: In all the inhibitor-bound structures the C-helix is in the 'αC out' position.
source: In all the inhibitor-bound structures the C-helix is in the 'αC out' position and the activation loop is collapsed into the kinase active site, burying the conserved BTK Y551 (Figure 2b–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2b-f showing crystal structures.

claim: In all the inhibitor-bound structures the activation loop is collapsed into the kinase active site, burying the conserved BTK Y551.
source: In all the inhibitor-bound structures the C-helix is in the 'αC out' position and the activation loop is collapsed into the kinase active site, burying the conserved BTK Y551 (Figure 2b–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2b-f showing crystal structures.

claim: The structure of the Tirabrutinib bound BTK shows that the activation loop adopts an alternative inactive loop conformation compared to the other inhibitor bound structures.
source: The structure of the Tirabrutinib bound BTK is the only structure that shows a difference; the activation loop in that complex adopts an alternative inactive loop conformation compared to the other inhibitor bound structures (Figure 2e and g).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2e and g showing crystal structures.

claim: Previous NMR and HDX-MS analysis of the interaction of BTK with a different panel of active site inhibitors has shown that there are differences between the solution and crystal behavior.
source: Previous NMR and HDX-MS analysis of the interaction of BTK with a different panel of active site inhibitors has shown that there are differences between the solution and crystal behavior (Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: BTK W395 within the linker region provides a useful probe to monitor the conformational state adopted by the kinase domain in solution.
source: We have previously shown that BTK W395 within the linker region (L) that precedes the kinase domain provides a useful probe to monitor the conformational state adopted by the kinase domain in solution (Joseph et al., 2020; Joseph et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Joseph et al., 2020; Joseph et al., 2017.

claim: The W395 indole 1H resonates at 10.21 ppm in the 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum of apo BTK linker-kinase domain, which adopts the active (αC in) conformation.
source: Assignments for the apo BTK linker-kinase domain, which adopts the active (αC in) conformation, show that the W395 indole 1H resonates at 10.21 ppm in the 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum (Figure 3, top panel, black spectrum).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing NMR spectra.

claim: An upfield shift in the BTK W395 side chain indole NH resonance is observed upon Ibrutinib binding and is consistent with the outward movement of the C-helix (αC out), and stabilization of the inactive kinase domain conformation by Ibrutinib.
source: An upfield shift in the BTK W395 side chain indole NH resonance is observed upon Ibrutinib binding and is consistent with the outward movement of the C-helix (αC out), and stabilization of the inactive kinase domain conformation by Ibrutinib (Figure 3, top panel, cyan spectrum Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib and Tirabrutinib stabilize the inactive kinase domain conformation in solution.
source: Comparing the tryptophan indole region of the 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectra for the BTK LKD inhibitor bound to Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib or Tirabrutinib with that of the apo BTK LKD protein shows that W395 undergoes an upfield shift in the presence of inhibitor (Figure 3), suggesting that, like Ibrutinib (Joseph et al., 2020) and consistent with the crystal structures, all of these inhibitors stabilize the inactive kinase domain conformation in solution.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing NMR spectra and a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: The Tirabrutinib-bound BTK kinase domain is likely adopting multiple kinase conformations in solution.
source: Interestingly, the Tirabrutinib bound spectrum shows several peaks corresponding to W395, suggesting that the Tirabrutinib-bound BTK kinase domain is likely adopting multiple kinase conformations in solution.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing multiple peaks for W395.

claim: The magnitude of the upfield shift in W395 resonance is smaller in both the Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib spectra compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib, which may reflect a relatively larger active state population in these samples.
source: Additionally, the magnitude of the upfield shift in W395 resonance is smaller in both the Tirabrutinib and Zanubrutinib spectra (compared to Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib), which may reflect a relatively larger active state population in these samples.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing different magnitudes of chemical shift changes.

claim: HDX-MS data confirms the stabilization of the inactive kinase conformation by Pirtobrutinib.
source: However, the fluorinated benzene ring in Pirtobrutinib, which is adjacent to the C-helix and W395 in the Pirtobrutinib bound structure, may cause changes in the local environment of W395 and thereby give rise to the unusual chemical shift change. Indeed, HDX-MS data (see below) confirms the stabilization of the inactive kinase conformation by Pirtobrutinib.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of the full-length BTK protein in the autoinhibited conformation was recently solved.
source: The structure of the full-length BTK protein in the autoinhibited conformation was recently solved (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2024.

claim: Electron density for both the N-terminal PHTH domain and proline-rich region is missing in the full-length BTK crystal structure, suggesting that the N-terminal region of BTK is dynamic.
source: However, electron density for both the N-terminal PHTH domain and proline-rich region is missing in this structure, suggesting that the N-terminal region of BTK is dynamic.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of electron density in the crystal structure.

claim: CryoEM, SAXS, and solution data all indicate that the PHTH domain is highly dynamic and likely transiently contacts multiple sites on the core SH3-SH2-kinase domain.
source: Indeed, CryoEM, SAXS, and solution data all indicate that the PHTH domain is highly dynamic and likely transiently contacts multiple sites on the core SH3-SH2-kinase domain (Figure 1b, Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2024 and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: For the majority of the inhibitor complexes studied, changes in deuterium incorporation are rarely observed in the PHTH domain suggesting that the PHTH domain dynamics are not affected by active site occupancy.
source: Additionally, our previous work (Joseph et al., 2020) has shown that for the majority of the inhibitor complexes studied changes in deuterium incorporation are rarely observed in the PHTH domain suggesting that the PHTH domain dynamics are not affected by active site occupancy.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibitor binding typically leads to decreased deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the kinase active site due to stabilization of this region in the presence of the bound inhibitor.
source: Inhibitor binding typically leads to decreased deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the kinase active site due to stabilization of this region in the presence of the bound inhibitor (Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibitors such as Ibrutinib that have allosteric effects lead to an increase in deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the BTK SH3 and SH2 domains as well as the SH2-kinase linker, indicating a shift away from the autoinhibited conformation.
source: Additionally, inhibitors such as Ibrutinib that have allosteric effects lead to an increase in deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the BTK SH3 and SH2 domains as well as the SH2-kinase linker, indicating a shift away from the autoinhibited conformation (Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: Intact mass analysis supports a single binding site on BTK for the covalent inhibitors.
source: Intact mass analysis supports a single binding site on BTK for the covalent inhibitors similar to what has been observed previously with Ibrutinib (Figure 4a, Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4a showing intact mass analysis and a citation to Joseph et al., 2020.

claim: Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib show decreased deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the kinase N-lobe and kinase activation loop similar to that observed previously with Ibrutinib.

claim: Decreased deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the kinase N-lobe and kinase activation loop is consistent with the binding of inhibitors in the kinase active site and stabilization of the inactive kinase conformation.

evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 4b, c, 5b-d and a citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: Pirtobrutinib binding to BTK shows decreased deuterium incorporation in peptides derived from the SH3 and SH2 domains, suggesting that Pirtobrutinib stabilizes the compact, autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.

source: To date, Pirtobrutinib is the only inhibitor that we have tested that uniformly stabilizes both the kinase domain as well as the regulatory domains in the inactive autoinhibited conformation.

claim: Each BTK inhibitor causes unique changes in the overall conformation of full-length BTK that is not readily predicted from crystal structures.
source: Thus, each BTK inhibitor causes unique changes in the overall conformation of full-length BTK that is not readily predicted from crystal structures.

claim: The BTK T474I mutant shows phosphorylation on Y551, however, it is lower than that of the WT protein.

claim: The T474I mutation reduces the activity of the BTK kinase.
source: The BTK T474I mutant shows phosphorylation on Y551, however, it is lower than that of the WT protein (Figure 6a and b) suggesting that the T474I mutation reduces the activity of the kinase.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant is completely inactive with no detectable phosphorylation on Y551 throughout the time course.
source: In contrast, the BTK L528W mutant is completely inactive with no detectable phosphorylation on Y551 throughout the time course (Figure 6c and d).

claim: The results on BTK T474I and L528W activity are consistent with previous activity reports on both mutants.
source: These results are consistent with previous activity reports on both the BTK T474I and L528W mutants (Wang et al., 2022; Handunnetti et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022; Handunnetti et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2022.

claim: Augmenting kinase activity is not the mechanism by which the BTK T474I or L528W mutations confer resistance.
source: Given that neither the BTK T474I, or the L528W mutant had increased catalytic activity, augmenting kinase activity is not the mechanism by which these mutations confer resistance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from activity assay data showing no increase in activity.

claim: The BTK T474I mutant shows increased deuterium incorporation within the kinase domain N-lobe β2-β3 strands and the activation loop.
source: Comparing the BTK T474I mutant to WT BTK, the BTK T474I mutant shows increased deuterium incorporation within the kinase domain N-lobe β2-β3 strands and the activation loop, but no changes elsewhere on the protein (Figure 6e, f and h).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6e, f and h showing HDX-MS data.

claim: Increased dynamics within the N-lobe of the BTK T474I mutant could potentially alter drug binding to the active site.
source: These increased dynamics within the N-lobe of the BTK T474I mutant could potentially alter drug binding to the active site.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on HDX-MS data showing increased dynamics.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant shows a decrease in deuterium incorporation in the kinase domain and the SH3 domain suggesting that the L528W mutation has a stabilizing effect on the full-length autoinhibited conformation of BTK.

evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6e, g and h showing HDX-MS data.

claim: The resonance corresponding to BTK A524 located close to T474 in the kinase active site shows line broadening in the BTK T474I mutant spectrum suggesting increased dynamics in the mutant.
source: The resonance corresponding to BTK A524 located close (~18 Å) to T474 in the kinase active site shows line broadening in the BTK T474I mutant spectrum suggesting increased dynamics in the mutant.

claim: The BTK W395 resonance in the BTK T474I mutant spectrum overlaps with that of the WT suggesting that the mutant kinase domain adopts an active conformation similar to that of the WT protein.
source: The BTK W395 resonance in the BTK T474I mutant spectrum overlaps with that of the WT suggesting that the mutant kinase domain adopts an active conformation similar to that of the WT protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing overlapping resonances.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant shows a small upfield shift in the W395 resonance, suggesting that the BTK L528W mutant kinase domain is shifted towards an inactive conformation compared to the WT protein.
source: The BTK L528W mutant on the other hand shows a small upfield shift in the W395 resonance, suggesting that the BTK L528W mutant kinase domain is shifted towards an inactive conformation compared to the WT protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing a chemical shift change.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant propagates BCR signaling despite being catalytically dead.
source: Previous studies have shown that the BTK L528W mutant propagates BCR signaling despite being catalytically dead (Wang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2022.

claim: PLCγ phosphorylation and calcium signaling are maintained in cells carrying the BTK L528W mutation.
source: PLCγ phosphorylation and calcium signaling are maintained in cells carrying this BTK mutation (Wang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2022.

claim: The BTK C481F/Y resistance mutant binds and activates the SRC family kinase HCK, thereby propagating signals from the BCR signaling pathway.
source: In that work the BTK C481F/Y resistance mutant was shown to bind and activate the SRC family kinase HCK, thereby propagating signals from the BCR signaling pathway (Dhami et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dhami et al., 2022.

claim: Activation of HCK by BTK C481F/Y requires phosphorylation on the BTK kinase activation loop, Y551.
source: This activation of HCK by BTK C481F/Y requires phosphorylation on the BTK kinase activation loop, Y551.
evidence: The claim is stated based on previous work on BTK C481F/Y.

claim: The phosphorylated Y551 is suggested to bind to the HCK SH2 domain, displacing the autoinhibited conformation of HCK, thereby activating the HCK catalytic function.
source: The phosphorylated Y551 is suggested to bind to the HCK SH2 domain, displacing the autoinhibited conformation of HCK, thereby activating the HCK catalytic function.
evidence: The claim is stated as a suggested mechanism based on previous work.

claim: The catalytically dead BTK L528W mutant is able to activate HCK.
source: As shown in Figure 7a and b, phosphorylation increased on both PLCγ and HCK in the presence of full-length BTK L528W, suggesting that the catalytically dead BTK mutant is able to activate HCK.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7a and b showing western blot data.

claim: Zanubrutinib bound WT BTK promoted increased phosphorylation levels on both PLCγ1 and HCK suggesting that drug-inactivated BTK also activates HCK.
source: Interestingly, Zanubrutinib bound WT BTK also promoted increased phosphorylation levels on both PLCγ1 and HCK suggesting that drug-inactivated BTK also activates HCK.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing increased phosphorylation.

claim: The mechanism of HCK activation by BTK L528W is distinct from what has been previously observed for the BTK C481Y/F resistant mutation.
source: This is distinct from what has been previously observed for the BTK C481Y/F resistant mutation where, compared to WT BTK, the C481Y/F mutant BTK preferentially engages HCK.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison with previous work on BTK C481Y/F.

claim: Phosphorylation on BTK Y551 is not required for HCK activation by the BTK L528W mutant.
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation on BTK Y551 is lower in the BTK L528W mutant compared to the WT BTK. This is likely due to the BTK kinase activation loop Y551 being less accessible to phosphorylation by HCK in the mutant (which adopts the autoinhibited conformation) compared to WT BTK (Figure 7a). Despite the lower pY551 level on BTK FL L528W mutant compared to BTK FL WT, the BTK FL L528W mutant is able to activate HCK similar to the BTK WT protein, suggesting that phosphorylation levels on BTK Y551 do not impact HCK activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from western blot data showing HCK activation despite lower Y551 phosphorylation.

claim: The BTK L528W/Y551F double mutant is able to activate HCK similarly to BTK L528W, suggesting that phosphorylation on Y551 is not required for HCK activation by BTK L528W.
source: Additionally, we tested whether the BTK L528W/Y551F double mutant is able to activate HCK. The BTK L528W/Y551F double mutant is able to activate HCK similarly to BTK L528W, suggesting that phosphorylation on Y551 is not required for HCK activation by BTK L528W (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1a showing western blot data.

claim: The isolated linker-kinase domain of BTK L528W does not activate HCK.
source: As shown in Figure 7c and d, the isolated linker-kinase domain of BTK L528W does not activate HCK.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7c and d showing western blot data.

claim: The regulatory domain/s of BTK are required for the activation of HCK by the BTK L528W mutant.
source: This suggests that the regulatory domain/s of BTK are required for the activation of HCK and that the isolated linker-kinase domain of BTK alone is insufficient for HCK activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from western blot data showing no HCK activation by the isolated kinase domain.

claim: The isolated linker-kinase domain of BTK alone is insufficient for HCK activation.
source: This suggests that the regulatory domain/s of BTK are required for the activation of HCK and that the isolated linker-kinase domain of BTK alone is insufficient for HCK activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from western blot data showing no HCK activation by the isolated kinase domain.

claim: The BTK C481Y/F resistant mutant requires the kinase domain for HCK activation.
source: This again is different from what has been previously reported; the BTK C481Y/F resistant mutant requires the kinase domain for HCK activation (Dhami et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dhami et al., 2022.

claim: The BTK L528W proline-depleted mutant does not activate HCK.
source: As shown in Figure 7e and f, the BTK L528W proline-depleted mutant does not activate HCK.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7e and f showing western blot data.

claim: The proline-rich region is present in both WT and mutant L528W BTK.
source: This data again emphasizes the difference between the mechanism of action of the BTK L528W mutant from the previously characterized BTK C481Y/F mutant. Additionally, this data is consistent with the observation that WT BTK can also activate HCK, as the proline-rich region is present in both WT and mutant L528W BTK.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation based on the protein sequence.

claim: The ability of both WT and L528W mutant BTK to activate HCK suggests that there must be additional reasons for the selection of the BTK L528W resistance mutation in patients.
source: The ability of both WT and L528W mutant BTK to activate HCK, however, suggests that there must be additional reasons for the selection of the BTK L528W resistance mutation in patients.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both WT and mutant activate HCK.

claim: Changes in protein levels have been shown to cause resistance in several cancers.
source: Changes in protein levels have been shown to cause resistance in several cancers (Pessoa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pessoa et al., 2022.

claim: Cellular protein levels can be altered due to changes in protein expression, stability or degradation, or changes at the RNA level.
source: Cellular protein levels can be altered due to changes in protein expression, stability or degradation, or changes at the RNA level (Pessoa et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pessoa et al., 2022.

claim: Protein yield after bacterial expression and purification of the full-length BTK L528W mutant is higher than that of the WT protein.
source: Interestingly, we note that protein yield after bacterial expression and purification of the full-length BTK L528W mutant is higher than that of the WT protein, suggesting that the L528W mutant is more stable than the WT protein.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from protein purification.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant is more stable than the WT protein.
source: As shown in Figure 7g, the BTK L528W mutant is more stable than the WT protein (a one-degree increase in Tm compared to the WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7g showing thermal shift assay data.

claim: The increased stability of the L528W mutant could result in increased protein levels, an increase in the lifetime of the protein, or altered protein trafficking in vivo.
source: The increased stability of the L528W mutant, albeit small, could result in increased protein levels, an increase in the lifetime of the protein, or altered protein trafficking in vivo, all of which would drive the interaction of the mutant protein with HCK, unlike the WT protein.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observed increase in stability.

claim: Disruption of inhibitor binding due to mutations is a classic mechanism by which resistance arises.
source: Disruption of inhibitor binding due to mutations is a classic mechanism by which resistance arises (Bhullar et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhullar et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2021.

claim: Tirabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib induce overall changes in deuterium incorporation for both WT BTK and the T474I mutant.
source: HDX-MS data show that Tirabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib induce overall changes in deuterium incorporation for both WT BTK and the T474I mutant (Figure 8a, b and c) These data suggest that the inhibitors are still capable of binding to the T474I mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8a, b and c showing HDX-MS data.

claim: The inhibitors Tirabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib are still capable of binding to the T474I mutant.
source: HDX-MS data show that Tirabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib induce overall changes in deuterium incorporation for both WT BTK and the T474I mutant (Figure 8a, b and c) These data suggest that the inhibitors are still capable of binding to the T474I mutant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing changes in deuterium incorporation.

claim: In the presence of Tirabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, or Pirtobrutinib, the magnitude of the protection in the kinase domain is consistently reduced in drug-bound T474I mutant as compared to the WT protein.
source: However, in the presence of Tirabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, or Pirtobrutinib, the magnitude of the protection in the kinase domain (N-lobe β2-β3 strands and activation loop) is consistently reduced in drug-bound T474I mutant as compared to the WT protein (Figure 8a, b, c and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8a, b, c and e showing HDX-MS data.

claim: The T474I mutation causes a reduction in inhibitor binding.
source: The differences in deuterium exchange for drug binding to WT and mutant BTK suggest that the T474I mutation causes a reduction in inhibitor binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing reduced protection in the mutant.

claim: The inhibitors do not stabilize the activation loop in the inactive conformation upon binding to the T474I mutant.
source: Specifically, the peptides derived from the kinase activation loop in particular do not show as much protection in the mutant relative to the WT suggesting that the inhibitors do not stabilize the activation loop in the inactive conformation upon binding to the T474I mutant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing less protection in the activation loop.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant does not show any change in deuterium incorporation in the presence of Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib or Pirtobrutinib, providing strong evidence that the BTK L528W mutant does not bind the inhibitors.
source: In stark contrast to the BTK T474I mutant, the BTK L528W mutant does not show any change in deuterium incorporation in the presence of Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib or Pirtobrutinib, providing strong evidence that the BTK L528W mutant does not bind the inhibitors (Figure 8d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8d showing HDX-MS data.

claim: Both the BTK T474I and the BTK L528W mutation impact inhibitor binding.
source: Taken together, both the BTK T474I and the BTK L528W mutation impact inhibitor binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing effects on inhibitor binding.

claim: The BTK T474I and the BTK L528W mutations disrupt binding to Zanubrutinib and Pirtobrutinib.
source: Indeed, these results are consistent with previous studies that show that the BTK T474I and the BTK L528W mutations disrupt binding to Zanubrutinib and Pirtobrutinib (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: The BTK T474I mutant undergoes minor changes in the presence of Zanubrutinib, suggesting that the mutant is binding weakly to the inhibitor.
source: Comparison of the Zanubrutinib bound WT BTK LKD spectrum to that of BTK T474I shows that the BTK T474I mutant undergoes minor changes in the presence of Zanubrutinib, suggesting that the mutant is binding weakly to the inhibitor (Figure 9a, left and middle panels).
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing minor spectral changes.

claim: Zanubrutinib does not stabilize the inactive conformation of the BTK T474I mutant kinase.
source: The W395 resonance shows little to no chemical shift change upon the addition of Zanubrutinib to the BTK T474I mutant, suggesting that this drug does not stabilize the inactive conformation of the mutant kinase (Figure 9a, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing no chemical shift change in W395.

claim: Tirabrutinib binds to both WT and BTK T474I mutant.
source: Spectral comparison of Tirabrutinib bound to WT and BTK T474I (Figure 9b, left and middle panels) shows drug-induced chemical shift changes for both complexes, supporting the conclusion from the HDX-MS data (Figure 8b) that the drug binds to both WT and mutant BTK.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9b showing NMR spectra and Figure 8b showing HDX-MS data.

claim: The BTK T474I mutation reduces binding to Tirabrutinib and the inactive kinase domain conformation (αC out) is less populated in the drug-bound mutant protein compared to WT BTK bound to Tirabrutinib.
source: Although BTK W395 gives rise to multiple peaks in the spectra of Tirabrutinib bound to both WT and T474I, the W395 resonances in the BTK T474I/Tirabrutinib complex are shifted upfield to a lesser extent compared to the same resonance in the WT/Tirabrutinib spectrum. This suggests that the BTK T474I mutation reduces binding to Tirabrutinib and the inactive kinase domain conformation (αC out) is less populated in the drug-bound mutant protein compared to WT BTK bound to Tirabrutinib.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing different chemical shift changes.

claim: Pirtobrutinib binds the BTK T474I mutant.
source: Spectral overlay of the Pirtobrutinib bound BTK T474I with the apo T474I protein shows pronounced chemical shift changes in the presence of the inhibitor, providing evidence consistent with the HDX-MS data (Figure 8c), that Pirtobrutinib binds the BTK T474I mutant (Figure 9c, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9c showing NMR spectra and Figure 8c showing HDX-MS data.

claim: The T474I mutation reduces affinity towards Pirtobrutinib.
source: However, unlike Pirtobrutinib bound to WT BTK, multiple W395 peaks are visible in the spectrum of Pirtobrutinib bound to BTK T474I. The resonance frequencies of the additional peaks are shifted toward that of the apo protein suggesting the possibility of fast exchange between inhibitor-bound and unbound states. These observations suggest that the T474I mutation reduces affinity towards Pirtobrutinib and is consistent with previously published SPR binding data (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing multiple peaks and is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: The BTK T474I mutation does not impact Ibrutinib or Fenebrutinib binding.
source: The NMR data suggest that the BTK T474I mutation does not impact Ibrutinib or Fenebrutinib binding (Figure 9d and f), but Acalabrutinib binding is reduced (Figure 9e).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9d and f showing NMR spectra.

claim: Acalabrutinib binding is reduced by the BTK T474I mutation.
source: The NMR data suggest that the BTK T474I mutation does not impact Ibrutinib or Fenebrutinib binding (Figure 9d and f), but Acalabrutinib binding is reduced (Figure 9e).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9e showing NMR spectra.

claim: The T474I mutation significantly reduces binding to Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib and Pirtobrutinib, retains binding to Ibrutinib and Fenebrutinib, and may have an adverse effect on Acalabrutinib binding.
source: Taken together, the T474I mutation significantly reduces binding to Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib and Pirtobrutinib, retains binding to Ibrutinib and Fenebrutinib, and may have an adverse effect on Acalabrutinib binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing different effects on different inhibitors.

claim: Disruption of drug binding is a possible mechanism by which the BTK T474I mutation escapes inhibition.
source: Given that the BTK T474I mutant retains activity (albeit reduced activity), disruption of drug binding is a possible mechanism by which this mutation escapes inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from activity and binding data.

claim: The BTK L528W mutation completely disrupts Zanubrutinib binding.
source: Spectral overlays of the BTK L528W mutant with and without Zanubrutinib show no chemical shift changes (Figure 9a, right panel) suggesting that the mutation completely disrupts inhibitor binding in complete agreement with the HDX-MS data (Figure 8d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9a showing NMR spectra and Figure 8d showing HDX-MS data.

claim: Tirabrutinib shows chemical shift changes in the BTK L528W mutant, but the changes are markedly different from that observed in the WT protein.
source: Tirabrutinib does show chemical shift changes, but the changes are markedly different from that observed in the WT protein (Figure 9b, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9b showing NMR spectra.

claim: Tirabrutinib could be binding to the BTK L528W in a different orientation.
source: In the L528W spectrum in the presence of Tirabrutinib, W395 shifts in the opposite downfield direction compared to the WT spectrum suggesting that Tirabrutinib could be binding to the BTK L528W in a different orientation.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on NMR data showing different chemical shift changes.

claim: The distinct chemical shift change in the BTK L528W/Tirabrutinib complex could be due to the mutated L528W residue altering the local chemical environment within the kinase.
source: Alternatively, the distinct chemical shift change could be due to the mutated L528W residue altering the local chemical environment within the kinase.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on NMR data showing different chemical shift changes.

claim: The Pirtobrutinib-bound BTK L528W spectrum shows a mixture of inhibitor-bound and unbound BTK kinase domains in solution, likely due to a reduction in Pirtobrutinib affinity caused by the L528W mutation.
source: The Pirtobrutinib-bound BTK L528W spectrum (Figure 9c, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) shows two resonance positions, one of which overlaps with the resonance in the apo protein and the other that corresponds to that of the mutant protein bound to Pirtobrutinib. This data suggests a mixture of inhibitor-bound and unbound BTK kinase domains in solution, likely due to a reduction in Pirtobrutinib affinity caused by the L528W mutation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing two resonance positions.

claim: The L528W mutation reduces binding to both Tirabrutinib and Pirtobrutinib.
source: Although the L528W mutation reduces binding to both Tirabrutinib and Pirtobrutinib, the NMR data suggests that it retains partial binding, unlike the HDX-MS data that suggests complete disruption of binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing some binding.

claim: The higher inhibitor concentrations used in the NMR experiments compared to the HDX-MS experiments likely explain the discrepancy between NMR and HDX-MS data for the L528W mutant.
source: The higher inhibitor concentrations used in the NMR experiments compared to the HDX-MS experiments likely explain this discrepancy.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on differences in experimental conditions.

claim: The BTK kinase domain adopts similar conformations in solution when bound to Tirabrutinib and Pirtobrutinib in the L528W mutant.
source: Interestingly, we note similarities between the BTK L528W Pirtobrutinib bound spectrum and that of the Tirabrutinib bound spectrum, suggesting that the BTK kinase domain adopts similar conformations in solution when bound to these different drugs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR data showing similar spectral features.

claim: The BTK L528W mutant retains binding to Fenebrutinib.
source: Additionally, the BTK L528W mutant retains binding to Fenebrutinib, however Ibrutinib, and Acalabrutinib binding are disrupted (Figure 9d–f, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9d-f showing NMR spectra.

claim: Ibrutinib and Acalabrutinib binding are disrupted by the BTK L528W mutation.
source: Additionally, the BTK L528W mutant retains binding to Fenebrutinib, however Ibrutinib, and Acalabrutinib binding are disrupted (Figure 9d–f, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 9d-f showing NMR spectra.

claim: The BTK L528W mutation significantly disrupts Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib binding.
source: Taken together, the BTK L528W mutation significantly disrupts Zanubrutinib, Tirabrutinib, and Pirtobrutinib binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from NMR and HDX-MS data showing disrupted binding.

claim: Three of the clinically approved BTK inhibitors (Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Tirabrutinib) shift the conformational ensemble of full-length BTK, destabilizing the autoinhibited conformation of the SH3 and SH2 domains to varying degrees.
source: Binding of BTK active site inhibitors can have long-range effects on the protein. Here, we build on earlier work to show that three of the clinically approved BTKi (Acalabrutinib, Zanubrutinib, and Tirabrutinib) shift the conformational ensemble of full-length BTK, destabilizing the autoinhibited conformation of the SH3 and SH2 domains to varying degrees (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Discussion and supported by reference to Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Pirtobrutinib led to the stabilization of the compact autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
source: In marked contrast, Pirtobrutinib led to the stabilization of the compact autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Discussion.

claim: The exposure or stabilization of the regulatory domains of BTK by active site BTK inhibitors can alter the interaction of BTK with ligands in vivo.
source: The exposure or stabilization of the regulatory domains of BTK by active site BTK inhibitors can alter the interaction of BTK with ligands in vivo.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observed conformational changes.

claim: BTK inhibitors have been shown to differ in their effectiveness at terminating signals downstream of the Fc receptor versus the B-cell receptor.
source: Indeed, BTK inhibitors have been shown to differ in their effectiveness at terminating signals downstream of the Fc receptor versus the B-cell receptor (Bender et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024).
